scenes.visual: Title card 'Catching Proteins on the Move' over the same cartoon cell from the first film, now relabelled 'pancreas cell that makes digestive enzymes'. Same world and COLOUR MAP as the first film: NUCLEUS DEEP BLUE, ROUGH ER TEAL with ribosome dots, GOLGI ORANGE stack, VESICLES GOLD, CELL MEMBRANE GREY, MITOCHONDRIA RED, ATP YELLOW sparks, marked protein a GOLD glow. Route strip at top as before. ADDED FOR THIS FILM: CONDENSING VACUOLES = larger pale-GOLD sacs beside the Golgi; STORAGE GRANULES = solid GOLD round granules near the cell's outer edge; a CLOCK counter top right reading 'minutes of chase'; a BAR CHART panel at right titled 'Where the marked grains are (% of counted grains)' with four bars: rough ER, Golgi vesicles, condensing vacuoles, storage granules. Only the values the lesson quotes at each time are drawn to height; the other bars stay light grey and are labelled 'other parts (not shown)'. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: How do we know proteins really travel in this order? The first film drew the route, from the rough E R to the Golgi to the cell membrane. But a drawing is not evidence.
scenes.caption: How do we know proteins really travel in this order? The first film drew the route, from the rough ER to the Golgi to the cell membrane. But a drawing is not evidence.
scenes.visual: The first film's final frame: the solid GOLD route line across the cell. A rubber stamp reading 'drawing' thumps onto it, then a question mark appears beside the route strip.
scenes.narration: How do we know proteins really travel in this order? The first film drew the route, from the rough ER to the Golgi to the cell membrane. But a drawing is not evidence.

scenes.tts: In 1967, James Jamieson and George Palade found a way to test it. They used thin slices of guinea pig pancreas. The cells they studied make digestive enzymes, not insulin. But they too send proteins out.
scenes.visual: Year '1967' and the names 'Jamieson and Palade' appear on screen. A cartoon guinea pig, then a thin slice of pancreas on a dish. Zoom to one cell; the label reads 'makes digestive enzymes (not a beta cell)'. Its teal ER, orange Golgi and gold granules match the first film's colours.
scenes.narration: In 1967, James Jamieson and George Palade found a way to test it. They used thin slices of guinea pig pancreas. The cells they studied make digestive enzymes, not insulin. But they too send proteins out.

scenes.tts: Here is the problem. A cell is always making new protein. If every protein carries a mark, the mark is everywhere, and you learn nothing about order. You need to mark just one batch.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the cell fills with GOLD glow at every stop at once, labelled 'everything marked: no order visible'. Then the glow clears and a single small group of dots is circled: 'mark one batch'.
scenes.narration: Here is the problem. A cell is always making new protein. If every protein carries a mark, the mark is everywhere, and you learn nothing about order. You need to mark just one batch.

scenes.tts: So they gave the slices a short pulse of a radioactive building block. Only proteins made during those few minutes carried the mark.
scenes.visual: The CLOCK counter appears reading 'pulse: 3 min'. GOLD-glowing building-block beads drip onto the slice for 3 minutes; new protein chains forming at the TEAL ER start to glow. The on-screen note: '3-minute pulse'.
scenes.narration: So they gave the slices a short pulse of a radioactive building block. Only proteins made during those few minutes carried the mark.

scenes.tts: Then came the chase: plenty of the ordinary building block. Proteins made after that carried no mark. The marked batch was now on its own.
scenes.visual: Plain grey beads now flood in. New chains at the ER stay grey. The clock resets to '0 minutes of chase'. The glowing batch stands out as a soft GOLD cloud of dots among grey ones.
scenes.narration: Then came the chase: plenty of the ordinary building block. Proteins made after that carried no mark. The marked batch was now on its own.

scenes.tts: They followed the batch in two ways. In one, broken cells were spun in a centrifuge, so their parts settled into layers. In the other, electron microscope pictures showed where radioactive grains sat.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a test tube in a spinning centrifuge; it stops and shows separate bands labelled 'ER pieces' (TEAL) and 'Golgi pieces' (ORANGE), one band glowing. Right: a grey electron-microscope-style cartoon of a cell section with small black dots labelled 'radioactive grains' sitting over the teal ER.
scenes.narration: They followed the batch in two ways. In one, broken cells were spun in a centrifuge, so their parts settled into layers. In the other, electron microscope pictures showed where radioactive grains sat.

scenes.tts: Time for a prediction. The clock reads zero minutes of chase. Right after the pulse, where do you predict most of the marked protein will be?
scenes.visual: Clock at '0 minutes of chase'. The bar chart panel appears with four empty bars and a question mark above them.
scenes.narration: Time for a prediction. The clock reads zero minutes of chase. Right after the pulse, where do you predict most of the marked protein will be?

scenes.visual: Hold on the empty bar chart; a timer ring fills over 5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Over the rough E R. At the start of the chase, most grains sat there. That is where ribosomes build new protein.
scenes.caption: Over the rough ER. At the start of the chase, most grains sat there. That is where ribosomes build new protein.
scenes.visual: Route strip: 'ribosome on rough ER' lights up. In the cell, the GOLD cloud of dots sits over the TEAL ER. Bar chart: the 'rough ER' bar rises to 86.3, labelled '86.3%'; the other three bars stay light grey.
scenes.narration: Over the rough ER. At the start of the chase, most grains sat there. That is where ribosomes build new protein.

scenes.tts: Minutes later, the marked batch had spread out. By seven minutes, Golgi vesicles held almost as many grains as the rough E R. Golgi vesicles are small vesicles at the Golgi's edge.
scenes.visual: Clock runs to '7 minutes of chase'. Part of the GOLD cloud drifts from the TEAL ER toward small GOLD vesicles at the edge of the ORANGE stack, while part stays over the ER. Bar chart redraws: 'rough ER' bar at 43.7, labelled '43.7%', and 'Golgi vesicles' bar at 43.0, labelled '43.0%', side by side with a small note 'nearly tied'; the other two bars light grey, 'other parts (not shown)'.
scenes.caption: Minutes later, the marked batch had spread out. By seven minutes, Golgi vesicles held almost as many grains as the rough ER. Golgi vesicles are small vesicles at the Golgi's edge.
scenes.narration: Minutes later, the marked batch had spread out. By seven minutes, Golgi vesicles held almost as many grains as the rough ER. Golgi vesicles are small vesicles at the Golgi's edge.

scenes.tts: Later still, the mark moved on again. The grains gathered in condensing vacuoles. These are storage granules that are still being formed.
scenes.visual: Clock runs to '37 minutes of chase'. The GOLD cloud collects in larger pale-GOLD sacs beside the Golgi, labelled 'condensing vacuoles (forming storage granules)'. Bar chart: 'condensing vacuoles' bar at 48.5, labelled '48.5%'; others light grey.
scenes.narration: Later still, the mark moved on again. The grains gathered in condensing vacuoles. These are storage granules that are still being formed.

scenes.tts: At the last time point shown, more than half the grains sat in finished storage granules. These hold the protein until the cell releases it.
scenes.visual: Clock runs to '117 minutes of chase'. The pale-GOLD sacs tighten into solid GOLD round granules, labelled 'storage (zymogen) granules'. Bar chart: 'storage granules' bar at 58.6, labelled '58.6%'; others light grey. Small note: 'chart shows 0, 7, 37 and 117 minutes only'.
scenes.narration: At the last time point shown, more than half the grains sat in finished storage granules. These hold the protein until the cell releases it.

scenes.tts: Each part's share of the mark peaked in turn. Rough E R, then Golgi vesicles, then condensing vacuoles, then storage granules. The chart shows only four moments of that journey.
scenes.caption: Each part's share of the mark peaked in turn. Rough ER, then Golgi vesicles, then condensing vacuoles, then storage granules. The chart shows only four moments of that journey.
scenes.visual: The four bar-chart frames appear side by side as small thumbnails in time order: 0, 7, 37, 117 minutes. Above them the route strip lights rough ER, Golgi vesicles, condensing vacuoles, then storage granules, in sync with the narration; a small note reads 'each part's own highest share; times between not shown'. Arrows run one way, left to right.
scenes.narration: Each part's share of the mark peaked in turn. Rough ER, then Golgi vesicles, then condensing vacuoles, then storage granules. The chart shows only four moments of that journey.

scenes.tts: These were digestive enzyme cells, not beta cells. Still, this experiment gave direct evidence for the order of stops that textbooks still draw. A drawing had become a measurement.
scenes.visual: The 'drawing' stamp from the first scene peels off the route line and is replaced by a stamp reading 'measured'. A small label stays in the corner: 'digestive-enzyme cells, not beta cells'.
scenes.narration: These were digestive enzyme cells, not beta cells. Still, this experiment gave direct evidence for the order of stops that textbooks still draw. A drawing had become a measurement.

scenes.tts: So how do we know the order? Mark one batch of new protein, then watch where it goes over time. Each stop's share peaks later than the stop before it.
scenes.caption: So how do we know the order? Mark one batch of new protein, then watch where it goes over time. Each stop's share peaks later than the stop before it.
scenes.visual: Fast replay: pulse beads glow, chase beads grey, the GOLD cloud spreads and moves ER to Golgi vesicles to condensing vacuoles to granules while the clock spins from 0 to 117 minutes of chase.
scenes.narration: So how do we know the order? Mark one batch of new protein, then watch where it goes over time. Each stop's share peaks later than the stop before it.

scenes.visual: End card with the logo hexagon character holding a stopwatch: 'Mark one batch, follow it, and the order of stops appears.'
